submitter: bugs_open/477 lane. Third round for this bug. Step A (corr b9fc0004) and step B (corr 3555a7a1) are both APPROVED and committed. This closes the blocker step B disclosed: the estate has no durable record of who a delivered site was delivered to.
rationale:
THE DEFECT IS WORSE THAN THE ABSENCE I REPORTED LAST ROUND, and the difference is the whole argument for a table rather than a documented convention.

Last round I disclosed that step B's sender can select nobody, because build_queue — the only permitted recipient source (651's header, corrected 2026-08-31 under bugs_open/420; sites.email explicitly forbidden) — has ZERO rows for idea.uk, the estate's only handed-over site, which was a rehearsal delivered to a hand-typed address. That stands. What I did not measure then, and the site_delivery_and_editor lane did, is what a reader GETS when they go looking.

`[MEASURED 2026-09-04, verified by me at the live row]` idea.uk carries `sites.email = 'idea.uk@contactforsales.com'` — a SITE MAILBOX. The delivery actually went to `aaa@designconsultancy.co.uk`. So there is no NULL to warn anybody: the obvious column is populated, well-formed, plausible and WRONG. Someone answering a support or refund question reads it and is confidently misled. An absence makes you go and look; a misleading value does not.

THE PLACEMENT IS AN OWNER RULING, RELAYED, AND I FLAG THAT IT REACHED ME SECOND-HAND. Owner, 2026-09-04, via the site_delivery_and_editor lane: a dedicated delivery record, written in the same statement as handed_over_at — NOT `sites.delivered_to`. The reason is the one that made me route the question to them rather than answer it myself: `sites` is read by a great many things and bugs_open/420's entire subject is controlling which address may live where. Customer PII does not belong on the widest-read table in the estate. I am recording the provenance of the ruling rather than presenting it as my own judgement.

WHY IT IS ONE STATEMENT AND NOT TWO. StampHandover's UPDATE claims the row (`WHERE handed_over_at IS NULL`, so exactly one caller wins). The recipient INSERT is a CTE on that same statement, selecting FROM the claimed rows — so it writes only when the claim was actually won, and it cannot be lost between two calls. Doing it as a follow-on INSERT would reintroduce precisely the shape this lane spent the day removing: a claim that succeeds and a second write that does not, leaving a delivered site whose recipient nobody knows. That is the same failure mode as the follow-up's own 'stamped but never sent', and I would rather not build a second instance of it in the commit that fixes the first.

AND THE STATE IS NOW UNREPRESENTABLE, not merely discouraged: StampHandover REFUSES an empty deliveredTo before touching the database. You cannot hand a site to a customer and not know which customer. One production caller (send_delivery_email_action.go) and it always has the address — the action already refuses an empty customer_email before claiming.

⚠ THE BACKFILL EXPIRES TODAY AND THAT IS WHY THIS ROUND IS NOW RATHER THAN TOMORROW. The only machine-readable copy of idea.uk's recipient is the delivery run's own row in orchestration_states, which is a ROLLING WINDOW: `[MEASURED 2026-09-04 13:59Z]` oldest row 1 day 02:11 old, and the idea.uk run (2026-09-03 19:30:31Z) had roughly seven hours left. Applied today, 778 captures it from the system's own record; applied tomorrow it captures nothing and the address has to be typed in by a human trusting a document. The fact itself is safe — it is in bugs_open/477 and in 778's header — but the ability to recover it mechanically is not.

⚠ ORDERING, AND IT IS THE ONE WAY THIS BREAKS PRODUCTION. 778 must be applied BEFORE an image carrying the new StampHandover rolls: the table is not optional to that statement, and without it every delivery fails at the claim. Migrations are live-on-apply and Go is inert until a roll, so applying today closes the window — but this is a real ordering constraint, stated plainly, and it is named in both the migration header and the Go comment.

WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING. This has not yet cost a real customer anything: one site has ever been delivered and it was ours. It is a hole waiting, not a hole leaking. But the next real delivery either came through an order (traceable) or did not (untraceable for ever, silently), and nothing tells you which.

ALSO IN THIS ROUND, from the same owner conversation: the follow-up interval is RULED at THREE DAYS (verbatim: 'I think the follow up should be 3 days'), superseding the 'a week or so' of the original suggestion, and 775's placeholder 7 becomes 3 in both the agent config and the pre_query. Plus two copy changes that are his observations, not my guesses, from performing the hosting steps himself: the letter now says setup takes about forty minutes and that slowness is not a fault (so at three days it reads 'here is what you need' rather than 'you have not done this'); and it carries a paragraph telling the customer to open their new address in a PRIVATE WINDOW, because a Netlify Drop site is private by default and looks perfectly public to the person who uploaded it — meaning a customer can press the confirm button in good faith with a site nobody can reach, and transfer_confirmed_at would then suppress the one message that might have told them.

plan.summary: Record who a delivered site was delivered to, in the same statement that claims the handover, and back-fill the estate's one historic delivery from the run log before that log ages out today. Plus the owner's 3-day interval ruling and two copy changes from his own hosting run.

edits.rationale: site_id is the PRIMARY KEY, which restates the once-only property: a site is delivered once, so it has at most one recipient, and a second delivery to a different address is a fact needing a decision rather than an UPDATE. recorded_by carries provenance because a backfilled row and a delivery-written row are not equally trustworthy. The backfill's verify DISTINGUISHES a zero caused by the window ageing out (RAISE WARNING, loud, not fatal — the table is worth having anyway) from a zero caused by my query being wrong (RAISE EXCEPTION), by asking independently how many recipients are still recoverable. A silently-empty backfill is the exact failure this whole bug is about. The scan is done ONCE into a temp table: `collected_data->'input_data' ? 'customer_email'` cannot use an index and one pass over 6,662 large jsonb rows MEASURED 102 seconds — the first draft did it per-site and did not finish, presenting as a hung psql rather than a slow query.

Takes deliveredTo, refuses it empty BEFORE touching the database (asserted by giving sqlmock no expectations, so any query fails the test), and records it in a CTE on the claim statement so the write happens only for a claim actually won. The claim predicate is untouched: `WHERE handed_over_at IS NULL` still decides the winner and no timestamp takes part, which is the property StampHandover's own comment exists to protect. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes it idempotent without weakening anything — the claim is what enforces once-only, and a conflict can only mean 778's backfill already holds the same fact.
edits.sketch:
WITH claimed AS (
  UPDATE sites SET handed_over_at=$2, live_link_expires_at=COALESCE(live_link_expires_at,$3)
   WHERE id=$1 AND handed_over_at IS NULL
  RETURNING handed_over_at, live_link_expires_at, transfer_confirmed_at IS NOT NULL AS confirmed
), recorded AS (
  INSERT INTO site_deliveries (site_id, delivered_to, delivered_at, recorded_by)
  SELECT $1, $4, claimed.handed_over_at, 'delivery-email' FROM claimed
  ON CONFLICT (site_id) DO NOTHING
) SELECT handed_over_at, live_link_expires_at, confirmed FROM claimed

edits.rationale: Threads deliveredTo to the stamp. A parameter rather than a field on LinkConfig, deliberately: LinkConfig is documented as the deployment-supplied half (hosts and payment URLs that differ per environment), and a customer's address is neither deployment-supplied nor environmental. Making PII an explicit argument also puts it where a reviewer of the CALLER can see it. One production caller.
edits.sketch:
func Claim(ctx, db, siteID, cfg LinkConfig, deliveredTo string, now time.Time) (Prepared, error)
	h, err := StampHandover(ctx, db, siteID, deliveredTo, now)

edits.rationale: Passes the customer address it already has and already validates. One line. The action refuses an empty customer_email well before the claim, so the new refusal inside StampHandover is a second belt rather than a new failure mode for this caller.
edits.sketch: prepared, err := delivery.Claim(ctx, params.DB, siteID, linkCfg, customerEmail, time.Now())

edits.rationale: The refusal is asserted to happen before the database is touched (sqlmock given no expectations). The statement is pinned to carry both halves. And the recipient is asserted to reach the database trimmed but otherwise verbatim — a handover that 'tidied' an address would record a different customer from the one emailed. The comment states in situ that a regex over SQL a mock received proves the statement was SENT, not that Postgres honours it, and names the rolled-back real-Postgres run that proves the behaviour.
edits.sketch:
mock.ExpectQuery(`(?s)WITH claimed AS.*UPDATE sites.*handed_over_at IS NULL.*INSERT INTO site_deliveries.*ON CONFLICT \(site_id\) DO NOTHING`).
	WithArgs(site, now.UTC(), now.UTC().Add(LiveLinkWindow), "customer@example.co.uk")

edits.rationale: The owner's interval ruling — three days, verbatim — replaces the placeholder 7 in both the agent config and the pre_query. The copy gains two things from his own hosting run: that setup takes about forty minutes and that slowness is not a fault, and the private-window check. The copy deliberately says 'a few days ago' rather than 'three days ago': the interval is CONFIG, and prose restating a config value is a lie waiting for the config to change. The schedule STAYS disabled and 775's verify still ABORTS if it is anything else — the interval being settled is not the same as someone having decided to email a real person today.

AND s.handed_over_at <= now() - interval '3 days'
